Women Suffrage. The political right of women to vote, a struggle spanning nearly a century in the United States before culminating in the Nineteenth Amendment in nineteen twenty. Though women were promised equality in the nation's founding, they were systematically excluded from political participation, property ownership, and legal personhood. The women's suffrage movement, beginning in earnest in eighteen forty-eight at Seneca Falls and carried forward by generations of activists, became the central struggle of the Progressive era, linking women's votes to broader demands for equality, labor rights, and reproductive autonomy.

The first organized demand for women's voting rights came at the Seneca Falls Convention in eighteen forty-eight, where Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott drafted the Declaration of Sentiments, modeled on the Declaration of Independence. Susan B. Anthony and Elizabeth Cady Stanton co-founded the National Woman Suffrage Association in eighteen sixty-nine, pioneering militant tactics including civil disobedience and symbolic arrests.

The Nineteenth Amendment was first introduced in Congress in eighteen seventy-eight and regularly reintroduced for forty-two years before finally passing in nineteen twenty—a remarkable persistence through multiple generational turnover. Carrie Chapman Catt, leading the National American Woman Suffrage Association, adopted a pragmatic state-by-state strategy that secured voting rights in numerous states before the federal amendment.

Wyoming in eighteen sixty-nine became the first territory to grant women the vote. By nineteen twenty, fifteen states had already enfranchised women, proving a political opening existed. The suffrage movement intersected with temperance, labor rights, and pacifism. Many suffragists were also Progressive reformers seeking to use women's votes to advance social legislation.

Southern white suffragists often collaborated with white segregationists and actively opposed Black women's voting rights, fracturing the movement's moral coalition. The Nineteenth Amendment, ratified in nineteen twenty, guaranteed that voting rights could not be denied on account of sex, though women's full political participation took decades more, faced with cultural barriers and voting suppression targeting Black women.
